extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of journalism history; historians and journalism scholars
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-level historical account of the origins and early development of newspapers and editors in colonial America, describing practices, conflicts with authority, and qualities that made journalism influential. Useful for understanding standards, pressures, and norms that shaped early American press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of news / currency
rubrics_metrics.description: The news organ must be up-to-date and avoid long delays in reporting (example: Campbell admitted he had been 'a little matter of thirteen months behind-hand with the news').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses public demand for current news (few coffee-houses, postmaster as central gossip source). Early American papers often relied on belated London copies; a publication far behind the news was seen as weak and uninteresting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and freedom of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's willingness to criticize practices and authorities (e.g., James Franklin's attack on inoculation) and to exercise 'courage and freedom of expression' is a virtue that can increase popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such editorial boldness could provoke official censorship, committees, imprisonment, or fines (e.g., General Court actions against the Courant), but it also attracted readers and shaped the paper's influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combativeness and representation of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism's highest development comes when it is 'combative, democratic and representative of the people' and acts as an active participant or leader in the fight for democratic ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers functioning as 'organs of public indignation and reform' achieve success for causes and influence for journalists; being combative and representative is linked to political impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality / bridging journalism and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism may gain authority and social standing by bridging the chasm between journalism and literature (examples: Addison, Swift, Steele 'teaching the English people to read').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic and literary virtues help journals establish political and social standing; modeling prose on respected essayists (Addison/Steele) improved quality (Benjamin Franklin imitated them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial voice / personal note
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion of a personal or 'personal note' by editors (sharp attacks, snappy accounts) became a recurring and valued feature of American journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell's attack on Brooker, Brooker's rejoinder — the personal tone helped define American editorial style and engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing 'by-authority' / avoiding offense
rubrics_metrics.description: A conservative editorial strategy is to publish 'by-authority' and print nothing likely to offend religious leaders or civil authorities (Campbell's practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach produced safe, often dull publications that avoided censorship but lacked the progressive spirit and influence associated with bolder journalism; the text contrasts this anti-pattern with more daring papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local reporting versus reliance on foreign extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance between local news and reprinting foreign extracts is a dimension of quality: many early papers were 'taken up with extracts from the London Flying Post and the London Gazette' while local news was often limited to deaths, sermons, and marine items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes public demand for news and the natural centrality of local reporting; reliance on foreign extracts was a safe introduction but limited a paper's local relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability: subscriptions, advertisements, circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper must be economically sustainable through subscriptions, advertisements, and sufficient circulation (Campbell's pleas for subscribers, admission that circulation was 'not over 300 copies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical business practices (taking ads, setting prices, collecting subscriptions) are essential; economic weakness led to appeals for public assistance and constrained editorial capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal constraints and defense against libel/censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers operate under legal risks (orders to submit manuscripts, suspensions, trials, imprisonment) and must sometimes mount legal defenses (examples: Courant ordered to submit, James Franklin imprisoned; Bradford defended himself against charges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text illustrates defensive tactics: legal argumentation, objecting to biased jurors, asserting printers' rights, and the broader struggle (Zenger-like) that shaped press freedom; awareness of libel and censorship contexts is a critical evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing public documents / official printing role
rubrics_metrics.description: A recognized role and standard for printers is producing public documents and laws: William Penn arranged that the colony's printer should be able 'to print the laws for the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding official printing roles (and the patronage that accompanied them) conferred influence but sometimes entailed constraints and expectations from authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban context for journalism development
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism 'would reach its highest development in the cities' where physical and social conditions facilitate interchange of thought and concerted action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues cities promote democratic public opinion and therefore more vigorous, influential journalism; context (city vs country) is an important factor when evaluating journalistic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional training and stylistic modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Training, apprenticeship, and stylistic modeling (e.g., James Franklin's London training; Benjamin Franklin modeling Addison and Steele) improve journalistic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter links London journalistic masters and training to improved prose, editorial technique, and readiness to take on a more influential press role in the colonies.
